newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Christopher defends U.S. role in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Christopher defends U.S. role in Africa.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Saturday said the United States would not "walk away from Africa" and indirectly criticised France for trying to maintain "exclusive patronage" on the continent.
In a speech at Witwatersrand University, he said much of Africa was at a fragile point and needed "the support of all its many friends, not the exclusive patronage of a few".
Christopher, on the fourth stop of a five-nation African tour, said: "All nations must cooperate, not compete, if we are going to make a positive difference in Africa's future."
"The time has passed when Africa could be carved into spheres of influence or when outside powers could view whole groups of states as their private domain," he added.
The comments relating to France were unusually strong for the U.S. secretary of state.
Officials said they were in response to France's scathing view of Christopher's tour of sub-Saharan Africa, the first he has made since taking office since 1993.
French officials were quoted this week in news reports as suggesting a proposed U.S.-led role on the African continent would trespass on traditional French territory.
Washington formally protested over the comments to Paris on Friday and France in turn complained about State Department criticisms on the same day.
U.S. officials travelling with Christopher were clearly miffed by the French broadside.
"The French are spectacularly uninformed about American politics," one official said.
He added: "The French are upset because they consider Africa to be their private domain. They feel threatened if others also want to make a contribution."
While in Africa, Christopher has promoted U.S. plans to organise an all-Africa force to be deployed in trouble spots.
He has also been encouraging African leaders to propose candidates to replace U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose reappointment Washington has vowed to veto.
In his speech Christopher confronted critics who argue the United States is disengaged form Africa, and asserted that "President Clinton is determined to intensify American engagement in Africa".
"I will not pretend to you that there is no debate in America about Africa's relative importance...(but) we cannot and will not walk away," he insisted.

Despite budget cuts, the administration over the past four years has sought to protect aid to Africa, given $600 million towards South Africa's transition from apartheid, helped Mali and Benin -- two former French colonies -- consolidate democracy, and been deeply engaged in peace efforts in Mozambique and Angola, he said.
Also, U.S. troops provided critical support for relief efforts in Rwanda and saved hundreds of thousands of lives in Somalia, he added.
Christopher lamented the problems facing African nations like Burundi. But his focus was much more on the future.

With the end of the Cold War, the demise of apartheid and African moves towards democracy "much of Africa is at a fragile mid-point, the point at which good leadership, sound policies and steady international support and engagement can make the greatest difference", he said.
Christopher said Washington was open to talks with Nigeria, but would take "appropriate steps if repression continues". He did not elaborate.
